primer.intro: A stack and a queue are the same thing - a shelf for values - governed by opposite disciplines. The stack is last in, first out: only the newest item is touchable, like a pile of plates. The queue is first in, first out: items leave in arrival order, like a ticket line. Nearly everything these structures do well follows from choosing the right discipline. Matching nested brackets is a stack job, because the closer you meet must answer the most recent opener. Serving requests fairly is a queue job. Both are a few lines over an array, and implementing them once by hand - top index, head and tail - buys the intuition every later topic spends.
whenToUse: Undo, backtrack, or match most-recent-first: the newest item matters, so stack.
Serve in arrival order - tickets now, breadth-first layers a few topics ahead - so queue.
Nested structure must be validated or peeled: brackets, parsers, editors.
Each element waits for the next bigger thing; a monotonic stack answers as it pops.
Operator precedence must be deferred: hold operators back until a stronger one forces them out.
primer.mentalModel: Everything is bookkeeping over an array. A stack is the array plus one top index: push writes above the top, pop reads the top and steps it down. A queue is the array plus head and tail: push writes at the tail, pop reads at the head, and both only move forward. Making a queue out of two stacks is a party trick with a lesson: pushes land in an in-box, pops come from an out-box, and only when the out-box runs empty is the in-box flipped over into it - each element crosses exactly once, so the average cost stays constant. The monotonic stack carries candidates in decreasing order; each new arrival pops every smaller candidate, handing each its answer on the way out.
mistakes: Popping or peeking with no empty check; the top index drifts below the floor and size turns to nonsense.
Flipping the in-stack into the out-stack on every operation - the amortized guarantee dies on the spot.
Shifting the entire array when the queue pops; move the head index and leave the data still.

example.title: Balanced brackets with a stack
example.explain: Openers wait on the stack; every closer must meet its own opener at the top, right now. The early return catches a closer with nothing open, the final check catches openers that went unanswered. A plain counter cannot do this job: it accepts the interleaved ([)] because totals match even though order is broken. The stack remembers both type and order, which is exactly what nesting means.

primer.practice: Open Practice with Implement Stack Using Arrays; the push-pop-top-size vocabulary it fixes is assumed by all five problems after it.

sections.title: One shelf, two disciplines
sections.text: Implement both once, bare-handed. The stack keeps a top index starting at -1: push increments then writes; pop reads then decrements; top reads without moving; size is top plus 1. The queue keeps head and tail: push writes at the tail and advances it, pop reads at the head and advances that, and wrapping both indices around the array's end turns it into a ring that reuses space forever. Agree on a sentinel - pop, top and front return -1 on an empty structure - and test that contract first, because real inputs hit it immediately. Every fancier structure in this topic is one of these two shelves plus a rule.

check.prompt: Starting from an empty stack: push 3, push 5, pop, push 8. What does top show now?

options.explain: The sentinel is for an empty stack; this one holds two items.
The pop removed 5; 8 was then pushed above 3 and is the newest item.
5 left the stack at the pop - it is gone.
3 is still there, but buried below 8; top sees only the newest.

reveal.solution: Trace the shelf: push 3 gives [3], push 5 gives [3, 5], pop removes the newest item 5 leaving [3], and push 8 gives [3, 8]. Top reads the newest item without removing it: 8. The stack now has size 2, and a further pop would return 8, then 3, then the empty sentinel -1.

sections.title: The monotonic stack
sections.text: To find each element's next greater element to the right, scan left to right keeping a stack of indices whose answer is still unknown - and keep their values in decreasing order. Each new value pops every smaller waiting index, and the moment of popping is the moment of answering: the newcomer is the first bigger thing those elements ever met. Then the newcomer joins the wait. Whatever remains when the scan ends answers -1. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the whole pass is linear even though single steps can pop many items. The same discipline, tilted to precedence instead of value, converts infix expressions to postfix: operators wait on the stack, and a weaker arrival flushes the stronger ones out.

quiz.prompt: Validate a string mixing ( ) [ ] { } so every closer matches its own opener. Which tool?

options.text: Compare counts of openers and closers
options.explain: Totals say balance is possible, nothing about type or order.

options.text: A stack of open brackets; each closer must match the popped top
options.explain: Nesting means the newest open bracket is the one a closer answers.

options.text: Three counters, one per bracket type
options.explain: Per-type totals still accept the interleaved ([)] - order is unchecked.

options.text: A queue of open brackets
options.explain: FIFO pairs a closer with the oldest opener; nesting demands the newest.

quiz.prompt: Build a queue when only stacks are available, with amortized constant operations. How?

options.text: Two stacks, flipped back and forth on every operation
options.explain: Perpetual flipping is the exact waste the lazy flip avoids.

options.text: One stack used upside down
options.explain: A stack has one usable end; attitude changes nothing.

options.text: Two stacks: pushes land in one, pops leave the other; flip only when the out side is empty
options.explain: Each element crosses once in its lifetime, so the average cost stays constant.

options.text: One stack, reversed in full before every pop
options.explain: Correct output, but every pop pays a linear reversal.

quiz.prompt: For every array element, find the first larger value to its right. Which plan is linear?

options.text: For each element, scan rightward until something bigger appears
options.explain: A descending array makes every scan run to the end: quadratic.

options.text: Sort and binary search each element
options.explain: Sorting forgets positions, and the question is positional.

options.text: A max-heap of all elements
options.explain: The global maximum answers nothing about what lies to one element's right.

options.text: A stack of waiting indices kept in decreasing value order; arrivals pop and answer them
options.explain: Push once, pop once per index - linear despite the nested-looking pops.

quiz.prompt: Convert infix like a+b*c to postfix. What role does the stack play?

options.text: It reverses the whole string
options.explain: Reversal alone produces neither correct order nor correct precedence.

options.text: Operators wait on it; an arrival pops those of higher or equal precedence first
options.explain: Operands stream straight to the output; the stack defers weaker operators.

options.text: It holds the operands
options.explain: Operands go directly out - only operators need to wait their turn.

options.text: It stores the final answer digit by digit
options.explain: Conversion rearranges symbols; nothing is evaluated.

quiz.prompt: From empty, run: push 4, push 7, top, pop, pop, pop, size - printing each result. What appears?

options.explain: top only peeks - it reports 7 without removing it, so the first pop still gets 7.
top shows 7, pops yield 7 then 4, the third pop hits empty (-1), size ends 0.
The third pop finds nothing - the sentinel -1 must appear, and size is 0.
That is queue order; a stack surrenders the newest first.

options.text: abc+*
options.explain: That multiplies by the sum b+c; precedence got inverted.

options.text: *+abc
options.explain: Operators leading is prefix notation, a different convention.

options.text: abc*+
options.explain: * binds tighter, so b*c happens first; + waits on the stack until the end.

options.text: ab+c*
options.explain: That is the postfix of (a+b)*c - parentheses would be needed.

quiz.prompt: Next greater element to the right for the array 2, 1, 3. What is printed?

options.explain: 1 also meets 3 as its next greater - the middle answer is 3.
3 is the first larger value for both 2 and 1; the final 3 finds nothing after it.
The last element has nothing to its right - it must answer -1.
That looked left; the question points right.

quiz.prompt: The monotonic-stack pass for next greater element over n items costs how much?

options.text: Linear - each index is pushed once and popped at most once
options.explain: Single steps may pop many, but the total pops over the run are bounded by n.

options.text: Quadratic, because one arrival can pop many items
options.explain: Charge each pop to the index popped - the sum across the whole run is n.

options.text: n log n
options.explain: No sorting or searching happens; only pushes and pops.

options.text: Constant
options.explain: Every element must at least be read once.

quiz.prompt: In the two-stack queue with the lazy flip, what does one pop cost?

options.text: Logarithmic
options.explain: Nothing halves; there is no tree or search here.

options.text: Always exactly one step
options.explain: The flip pops are real work - the claim is about the average, so amortized.

options.text: Amortized constant - each element crosses between stacks once in its lifetime
options.explain: A single pop may pay for a flip, but the total crossings equal total pushes.

options.text: Always linear
options.explain: Linear happens only on the rare pop that triggers a flip, and it is prepaid.

quiz.prompt: This checker accepts the string ([)]. What is the bug?

options.text: A counter checks totals only; a stack must pair each closer with the top opener
options.explain: ([)] balances every count yet interleaves types - only order-aware memory sees it.

options.text: The counter must also never dip below zero
options.explain: That extra guard rejects )( but still accepts the interleaved ([)].

options.text: Three separate counters are needed
options.explain: Per-type totals still miss interleaving; the flaw is order, not arithmetic.

options.text: The loop skips the last character
options.explain: The loop reads every character; its memory is what falls short.

quiz.prompt: After one push and two pops, size() reports -1. What is the bug?

options.text: size must return t, without the plus 1
options.explain: size equal to t plus 1 is right by design; the drift below -1 is the fault.

options.text: v must be read after the decrement
options.explain: Reading after the step returns the slot below the top - a different bug.

options.text: No empty guard: the second pop drags t to -2; return the sentinel and leave t alone
options.explain: Guard t at -1 first - return -1 without decrementing.

options.text: push is the broken one
options.explain: A push that pairs with one pop leaves t consistent; the damage needs the second pop.

quiz.prompt: Which case most deserves the first test for any stack or queue you implement?

options.text: A million pushes in a row
options.explain: Capacity stress is useful later; the empty contract fails earlier and cheaper.

options.text: Pushing negative values
options.explain: Values flow through untouched; the discipline cares about order only.

options.text: Alternating push and pop forever
options.explain: A fine soak test, but it rarely finds what the first empty pop finds instantly.

options.text: pop, top and front on a freshly created empty structure
options.explain: The -1 sentinel contract and index floors break here first, before any happy path.
